message.content: {"schema_version":"teaching-unit.v0.4.0","input_manifest_sha256":"9a388b8b36e7f3e6e7cde2f0d97850d1ebd45451597d3d431a2b5d8d2baeef2f","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-nv-class-c:lineage:55","source_registry_sha256":"3e184808e042e052d0c78d0dff47c50b34a56560f428649c492afe10bc7ba712","units":[{"unit_id":"sec03-u01","module_id":"sec03-m01","objective_ids":["sec03-u01"],"title":{"text":"Seat belts and the law","fact_ids":["sec03-F01","sec03-F02","sec03-F03"]},"why_how":[{"text":"Seat belts are the best protection against injury or death in a crash, and Nevada requires them by law.","fact_ids":["sec03-F01"]},{"text":"Unbelted drivers still make up a large share of Nevada highway deaths, so the rule saves real lives.","fact_ids":["sec03-F02","sec03-F03"]},{"text":"Older cars carry different belts depending on their model year, which explains why some classic cars have front lap belts only.","fact_ids":["sec03-F04","sec03-F05","sec03-R03"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"A family of four rides in a car: the driver, an adult passenger, and two children aged eight and ten.","fact_ids":["sec03-F06"]},"reasoning":{"text":"The driver and every passenger aged six or older must wear a safety belt whenever the vehicle has one.","fact_ids":["sec03-F06"]},"result":{"text":"All four must be belted, because both children are older than six.","fact_ids":["sec03-F06"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking seat belts are only a recommendation for adults in the back seat.","fact_ids":["sec03-F01","sec03-F06"]},"correction":{"text":"Belts are required by law, and the rule covers the driver and every passenger six or older wherever they sit.","fact_ids":["sec03-F01","sec03-F06"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Six and up, everyone buckles.","fact_ids":["sec03-F06"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"A classic car from model year nineteen sixty-nine has front lap belts only. Does that meet the equipment rule for its year?","fact_ids":["sec03-F04","sec03-R03"]},"answer":{"text":"Yes; the requirement for that year is lap belts for the front-seat passengers.","fact_ids":["sec03-F04","sec03-R03"]},"rationale":{"text":"From nineteen sixty-eight, cars need front-seat lap belts; the wider rule with all lap belts and front shoulder harnesses starts with nineteen seventy models.","fact_ids":["sec03-F04","sec03-F05","sec03-R03"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec03-u01-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Why we buckle up","fact_ids":["sec03-F01","sec03-F06"]},"lines":[{"text":"Belts are your best protection.","fact_ids":["sec03-F01","sec03-F06"]},{"text":"Nevada requires them by law.","fact_ids":["sec03-F01","sec03-F06"]}],"narration":{"text":"This lesson begins the chapter on buckling up. Nevada calls seat belts your best protection against injury or death in a crash, and wearing them is required by law, not just advised. We will look at what the numbers say about drivers who go unbelted, which seat belts cars must have depending on their model year, and who in the vehicle must buckle up. The next lessons turn to children, pets and child seats, but everything starts here, with the simple rule that every driver and older passenger wears a belt on every trip.","fact_ids":["sec03-F01","sec03-F06"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec03-u01-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"The cost of going unbelted","fact_ids":["sec03-F02","sec03-F03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Nearly a quarter of highway deaths.","fact_ids":["sec03-F02","sec03-F03"]},{"text":"Hundreds killed in five years.","fact_ids":["sec03-F02","sec03-F03"]}],"narration":{"text":"The handbook backs the law with numbers. In twenty twenty, drivers who were not wearing seat belts made up a little more than twenty-three percent of Nevada highway fatalities, an increase of a little over one percent compared with twenty sixteen. From twenty sixteen through twenty twenty, three hundred forty-five unbelted vehicle occupants were killed in Nevada. These are people who might have survived with a belt on. The point is not to memorize every decimal but to understand that going unbelted is a common and deadly choice, which is why the law treats it as a requirement.","fact_ids":["sec03-F02","sec03-F03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec03-u01-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Belts by model year","fact_ids":["sec03-F04","sec03-F05","sec03-R03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Nineteen sixty-eight: front lap belts.","fact_ids":["sec03-F04","sec03-F05","sec03-R03"]},{"text":"Nineteen seventy: all lap belts.","fact_ids":["sec03-F04","sec03-F05","sec03-R03"]},{"text":"Nineteen seventy: front shoulder harnesses.","fact_ids":["sec03-F04","sec03-F05","sec03-R03"]}],"narration":{"text":"Cars must carry seat belts based on their model year. A car of model year nineteen sixty-eight or newer must have lap-type seat belts for the front-seat passengers. A car of model year nineteen seventy or newer must have lap-type belts for every passenger plus shoulder harnesses for the front seat. So the earlier rule covers only the front, and the later rule reaches every seat and adds the shoulder harness up front. Most cars on the road today are far newer than either date, but the rule explains why some classic cars have fewer belts than modern ones.","fact_ids":["sec03-F04","sec03-F05","sec03-R03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec03-u01-s4","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Two model years, two rules","fact_ids":["sec03-R03","sec03-F04","sec03-F05"]},"lines":[{"text":"Sixty-eight covers the front only.","fact_ids":["sec03-R03","sec03-F04","sec03-F05"]},{"text":"Seventy covers everyone, plus front harnesses.","fact_ids":["sec03-R03","sec03-F04","sec03-F05"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a trap with two nearby years. It is easy to remember that old cars need belts and forget which year added what. Nineteen sixty-eight is the front-only rule: lap belts for the front-seat passengers. Nineteen seventy is the wider rule: lap belts for every passenger and shoulder harnesses for the front seat. If a question gives you a car from nineteen sixty-nine, only the front lap-belt rule applies. If it gives you a car from nineteen seventy or later, every passenger needs a lap belt and the front seat needs shoulder harnesses too.","fact_ids":["sec03-R03","sec03-F04","sec03-F05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec03-u01-s5","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check a classic car","fact_ids":["sec03-F04","sec03-R03","sec03-F05"]},"lines":[{"text":"A nineteen sixty-nine car.","fact_ids":["sec03-F04","sec03-R03","sec03-F05"]},{"text":"Front lap belts only.","fact_ids":["sec03-F04","sec03-R03","sec03-F05"]},{"text":"Does it meet its rule?","fact_ids":["sec03-F04","sec03-R03","sec03-F05"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: a classic car from model year nineteen sixty-nine has front lap belts only, with no shoulder harnesses and no rear belts. Does that meet the equipment rule for its model year? Work it out before reading on. Yes, it does. From nineteen sixty-eight on, cars must have lap belts for the front-seat passengers, and that is what this car has. The wider rule, with lap belts for every passenger and front shoulder harnesses, applies only to cars of model year nineteen seventy or newer, so it does not reach this car.","fact_ids":["sec03-F04","sec03-R03","sec03-F05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec03-u01-s6","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Belt rules recap","fact_ids":["sec03-F01","sec03-F02","sec03-F03","sec03-F04","sec03-F05","sec03-F06"]},"lines":[{"text":"Required by law.","fact_ids":["sec03-F01","sec03-F02","sec03-F03","sec03-F04","sec03-F05","sec03-F06"]},{"text":"Six and older buckle up.","fact_ids":["sec03-F01","sec03-F02","sec03-F03","sec03-F04","sec03-F05","sec03-F06"]},{"text":"Model year sets the equipment.","fact_ids":["sec03-F01","sec03-F02","sec03-F03","sec03-F04","sec03-F05","sec03-F06"]}],"narration":{"text":"To sum up, Nevada requires seat belts by law and calls them your best protection in a crash. Unbelted drivers make up a large share of highway deaths, and hundreds of unbelted occupants were killed in recent years. Cars from nineteen sixty-eight on need front lap belts, and cars from nineteen seventy on need lap belts for everyone plus front shoulder harnesses. The driver and every passenger aged six or older must wear a belt whenever the vehicle has one. In the next lesson we look at children under six, unattended children, and pets left in vehicles.","fact_ids":["sec03-F01","sec03-F02","sec03-F03","sec03-F04","sec03-F05","sec03-F06"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"}]},{"unit_id":"sec03-u02","module_id":"sec03-m02","objective_ids":["sec03-u02"],"title":{"text":"Children, pets and the law","fact_ids":["sec03-F07","sec03-F08","sec03-R04"]},"why_how":[{"text":"Children need more than an adult belt, and the law sets clear age and height lines for restraints.","fact_ids":["sec03-F07","sec03-F09"]},{"text":"Leaving a child or a pet in a vehicle can be a crime, so drivers need to know when it is allowed.","fact_ids":["sec03-F11","sec03-F12"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"A parent drives with a five-year-old who is already fifty-nine inches tall.","fact_ids":["sec03-F07","sec03-R01"]},"reasoning":{"text":"Children under six, and children shorter than fifty-seven inches, must ride in an approved child restraint.","fact_ids":["sec03-F07","sec03-R01"]},"result":{"text":"The child is under six, so a restraint is still required even though the child is taller than fifty-seven inches.","fact_ids":["sec03-F07","sec03-R01"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking a child can switch to an adult belt the day they turn six.","fact_ids":["sec03-R01","sec03-F07"]},"correction":{"text":"Age six starts the belt rule, but a child still under fifty-seven inches keeps needing a restraint.","fact_ids":["sec03-R01","sec03-F07"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Under two rear-facing; under six or short, restrained.","fact_ids":["sec03-F09","sec03-F07"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"A thirteen-year-old sibling stays in the car, keeping a four-year-old in sight, while a parent runs into a store on a hot day. Is the parent breaking the unattended-child rule?","fact_ids":["sec03-F11","sec03-R02"]},"answer":{"text":"No, because someone at least twelve is supervising within sight.","fact_ids":["sec03-F11","sec03-R02"]},"rationale":{"text":"The rule protects children seven or younger, and its exception is supervision by a person at least twelve who keeps the child in sight.","fact_ids":["sec03-F11","sec03-R02"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec03-u02-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Protecting the youngest riders","fact_ids":["sec03-F07","sec03-F11","sec03-F12"]},"lines":[{"text":"Child restraints by age and height.","fact_ids":["sec03-F07","sec03-F11","sec03-F12"]},{"text":"Unattended children and pets.","fact_ids":["sec03-F07","sec03-F11","sec03-F12"]}],"narration":{"text":"This lesson covers the rules that protect children and pets in vehicles. Adult seat belts are not built for small bodies, so Nevada law requires approved child restraints for young children, with an extra rule for babies and toddlers. We will also look at what never to do with a child passenger, the penalties for breaking the restraint law, and the laws against leaving a young child or a dog or cat alone in a vehicle. Several of these rules turn on specific ages, so pay attention to which age belongs to which rule, because they are easy to mix up.","fact_ids":["sec03-F07","sec03-F11","sec03-F12"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec03-u02-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Child restraint rules","fact_ids":["sec03-F07","sec03-F09","sec03-F10"]},"lines":[{"text":"Under six or under fifty-seven inches: restraint.","fact_ids":["sec03-F07","sec03-F09","sec03-F10"]},{"text":"Under two: rear-facing in back.","fact_ids":["sec03-F07","sec03-F09","sec03-F10"]},{"text":"No laps, no shared belts.","fact_ids":["sec03-F07","sec03-F09","sec03-F10"]}],"narration":{"text":"Children under six, and children shorter than fifty-seven inches, must ride in an approved child restraint system. A child under two must ride in a rear-facing child restraint system in the back seat. Never hold a child on your lap, and never share one safety belt between a child and another person. Holding a child in your arms may feel safe, but in a crash the force is far too strong to hold on. Each child needs a properly fitting restraint or, once old and tall enough, a belt of their own, never a shared one. Secure each child separately.","fact_ids":["sec03-F07","sec03-F09","sec03-F10"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec03-u02-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Penalties for the driver","fact_ids":["sec03-F08","sec03-R04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Fines or community service.","fact_ids":["sec03-F08","sec03-R04"]},{"text":"Possible license suspension.","fact_ids":["sec03-F08","sec03-R04"]},{"text":"Or a combination.","fact_ids":["sec03-F08","sec03-R04"]}],"narration":{"text":"Failing to restrain a child under six or under fifty-seven inches can lead to fines, community service, a license suspension, or a combination of these. That last item matters: the restraint law reaches the driver's license itself. A driver who carries an unrestrained young child is not just risking a ticket, but possibly the right to drive. So the child restraint rule is enforced on the driver, and the consequences can follow the driver well beyond a single fine. Keeping a properly fitted restraint in the car for every young child avoids every one of these penalties.","fact_ids":["sec03-F08","sec03-R04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec03-u02-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Unattended children and pets","fact_ids":["sec03-F11","sec03-R02","sec03-F12","sec03-F13"]},"lines":[{"text":"Child seven or younger: never alone at risk.","fact_ids":["sec03-F11","sec03-R02","sec03-F12","sec03-F13"]},{"text":"Exception: supervisor twelve or older in sight.","fact_ids":["sec03-F11","sec03-R02","sec03-F12","sec03-F13"]},{"text":"Dogs and cats: not in extreme heat or cold.","fact_ids":["sec03-F11","sec03-R02","sec03-F12","sec03-F13"]}],"narration":{"text":"Do not leave a child aged seven or younger alone in a vehicle when conditions pose a significant risk to the child's health and safety, unless a person at least twelve years old is supervising within sight. Leaving a dog or cat unattended in a vehicle during extreme heat or cold is also illegal, and police officers, firefighters and other officials are allowed to use reasonable force to free the animal. Breaking either the unattended-child law or the unattended-pet law is a misdemeanor. So both laws carry the same level of offense, even though they protect different passengers.","fact_ids":["sec03-F11","sec03-R02","sec03-F12","sec03-F13"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec03-u02-s5","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Ages and triggers","fact_ids":["sec03-R01","sec03-R02","sec03-R05"]},"lines":[{"text":"Two, six and fifty-seven inches.","fact_ids":["sec03-R01","sec03-R02","sec03-R05"]},{"text":"Seven for the child, twelve for the watcher.","fact_ids":["sec03-R01","sec03-R02","sec03-R05"]},{"text":"Risk for children, heat or cold for pets.","fact_ids":["sec03-R01","sec03-R02","sec03-R05"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a trap built from several numbers. Age two marks the rear-facing back-seat rule. Age six marks both the start of the adult belt requirement and the end of the under-six restraint rule, though a child still under fifty-seven inches keeps needing a restraint. In the unattended-child law, seven is the child's age limit and twelve is the supervisor's minimum age. And the triggers differ: the child rule turns on significant risk to health and safety, while the pet rule turns on extreme heat or cold. Match each number to its rule before you answer.","fact_ids":["sec03-R01","sec03-R02","sec03-R05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec03-u02-s6","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check a store errand","fact_ids":["sec03-F11","sec03-R02"]},"lines":[{"text":"A four-year-old in the car.","fact_ids":["sec03-F11","sec03-R02"]},{"text":"A thirteen-year-old watching.","fact_ids":["sec03-F11","sec03-R02"]},{"text":"Is the rule broken?","fact_ids":["sec03-F11","sec03-R02"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: on a hot day, a parent runs into a store while a thirteen-year-old sibling stays in the car, keeping a four-year-old in sight. Is the parent breaking the unattended-child rule? Think about both ages before reading on. No, the rule is not broken. The rule protects children seven or younger from being left alone at significant risk, and its exception is supervision by a person at least twelve years old who keeps the child in sight. A thirteen-year-old watching the child meets that exception, though a nine-year-old would not.","fact_ids":["sec03-F11","sec03-R02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec03-u02-s7","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Children and pets recap","fact_ids":["sec03-F07","sec03-F09","sec03-F10","sec03-F08","sec03-F11","sec03-F12","sec03-F13","sec03-R01"]},"lines":[{"text":"Restraints under six or under fifty-seven inches.","fact_ids":["sec03-F07","sec03-F09","sec03-F10","sec03-F08","sec03-F11","sec03-F12","sec03-F13","sec03-R01"]},{"text":"Rear-facing in back under two.","fact_ids":["sec03-F07","sec03-F09","sec03-F10","sec03-F08","sec03-F11","sec03-F12","sec03-F13","sec03-R01"]},{"text":"Unattended child or pet: misdemeanor.","fact_ids":["sec03-F07","sec03-F09","sec03-F10","sec03-F08","sec03-F11","sec03-F12","sec03-F13","sec03-R01"]}],"narration":{"text":"Let us review. Children under six or shorter than fifty-seven inches ride in an approved child restraint, and children under two ride rear-facing in the back seat. Never hold a child on your lap or share a belt. Breaking the restraint rule can bring fines, community service or a license suspension. A child seven or younger may not be left alone at significant risk unless someone twelve or older supervises in sight, and a dog or cat may not be left in extreme heat or cold. Both offenses are misdemeanors. Next, we look at choosing and placing child seats.","fact_ids":["sec03-F07","sec03-F09","sec03-F10","sec03-F08","sec03-F11","sec03-F12","sec03-F13","sec03-R01"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"}]},{"unit_id":"sec03-u03","module_id":"sec03-m03","objective_ids":["sec03-u03"],"title":{"text":"Choosing and placing child seats","fact_ids":["sec03-F14","sec03-F15","sec03-F16"]},"why_how":[{"text":"The right seat, installed the right way and in the right spot, is what turns a child restraint into real protection.","fact_ids":["sec03-R08","sec03-F18"]},{"text":"Airbags save adults but can badly hurt infants and passengers sitting too close.","fact_ids":["sec03-F20","sec03-F21"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"A parent with a newborn has a car with a passenger-side airbag and wants the baby up front to keep an eye on her.","fact_ids":["sec03-F21","sec03-R06"]},"reasoning":{"text":"An infant must never ride in front of a passenger-side airbag, because it bursts out at very high speed and can strike the back of the baby's head.","fact_ids":["sec03-F21"]},"result":{"text":"The baby rides rear-facing in the back seat instead, where children are generally safest.","fact_ids":["sec03-F21","sec03-F17","sec03-F18"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking a rear-facing seat makes it safe to put an infant in front of a passenger airbag.","fact_ids":["sec03-F21","sec03-R06"]},"correction":{"text":"The airbag can strike the back of the baby's head through the safety seat, so an infant never rides in front of a passenger airbag.","fact_ids":["sec03-F21","sec03-R06"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Babies back and facing back.","fact_ids":["sec03-F17","sec03-F18"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"Before a road trip, what three things should a parent confirm about a child's car seat?","fact_ids":["sec03-R08","sec03-F15","sec03-F16"]},"answer":{"text":"It is DOT-approved, it fits the child's size and weight, and it is installed as the maker or NHTSA directs.","fact_ids":["sec03-R08","sec03-F15","sec03-F16"]},"rationale":{"text":"Safe child travel needs an approved restraint, a seat that fits the child, and an installation that follows the manufacturer or NHTSA.","fact_ids":["sec03-R08","sec03-F15","sec03-F16"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec03-u03-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"The right seat, the right way","fact_ids":["sec03-F14","sec03-F17","sec03-R08","sec03-F18"]},"lines":[{"text":"Booster and rear-facing seats.","fact_ids":["sec03-F14","sec03-F17","sec03-R08","sec03-F18"]},{"text":"Three checks before travel.","fact_ids":["sec03-F14","sec03-F17","sec03-R08","sec03-F18"]},{"text":"Seating and airbags.","fact_ids":["sec03-F14","sec03-F17","sec03-R08","sec03-F18"]}],"narration":{"text":"This lesson is about choosing a child seat, installing it, and deciding where the child sits. We will compare booster seats with rear-facing infant seats, walk through the checks to make before travelling with a child, and look at why the back seat is generally the safest place. Then we turn to airbags. They protect adults, but they can badly hurt unbuckled passengers, passengers sitting too close, and infants placed in front of them. By the end you should know how to pick, fit and place a seat so it actually protects the child it carries.","fact_ids":["sec03-F14","sec03-F17","sec03-R08","sec03-F18"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec03-u03-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Two kinds of seats","fact_ids":["sec03-F14","sec03-F17","sec03-R07"]},"lines":[{"text":"Booster: lifts the child for the vehicle belt.","fact_ids":["sec03-F14","sec03-F17","sec03-R07"]},{"text":"Rear-facing: holds the infant itself.","fact_ids":["sec03-F14","sec03-F17","sec03-R07"]},{"text":"Rear-facing protects head, neck and spine.","fact_ids":["sec03-F14","sec03-F17","sec03-R07"]}],"narration":{"text":"Booster seats and belt-positioning seats raise or position a child so the vehicle's seat belt can secure the child safely. Infants, by contrast, are always buckled in facing the rear, because a rear-facing seat supports the baby's head and shields the neck and spine in most crashes. So the two seats work in different ways: a booster works with the vehicle's own belt, while a rear-facing seat holds the infant itself. Choosing between them depends on the child, and the infant always starts out in the rear-facing seat for that head, neck and spine protection.","fact_ids":["sec03-F14","sec03-F17","sec03-R07"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec03-u03-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Three checks before travel","fact_ids":["sec03-F15","sec03-F16","sec03-R08"]},"lines":[{"text":"Approved by the federal transportation department.","fact_ids":["sec03-F15","sec03-F16","sec03-R08"]},{"text":"Fits the child's size and weight.","fact_ids":["sec03-F15","sec03-F16","sec03-R08"]},{"text":"Installed as the maker or NHTSA directs.","fact_ids":["sec03-F15","sec03-F16","sec03-R08"]}],"narration":{"text":"Before travelling with a child, check that the restraint is approved by the US Department of Transportation under the Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards and suits the child's size and weight. A child restraint must also be installed safely and securely, following the manufacturer's instructions or another method approved by NHTSA. Put together, safe child travel needs three checks: a DOT-approved restraint, a seat that fits the child's size and weight, and an installation that follows the manufacturer or NHTSA. Skipping any one of the three can leave the child unprotected in a crash.","fact_ids":["sec03-F15","sec03-F16","sec03-R08"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec03-u03-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Where children should sit","fact_ids":["sec03-F18","sec03-F19","sec03-F20"]},"lines":[{"text":"The back seat is generally safest.","fact_ids":["sec03-F18","sec03-F19","sec03-F20"]},{"text":"Older child in front: seat fully back.","fact_ids":["sec03-F18","sec03-F19","sec03-F20"]},{"text":"Full harness or fitted belt.","fact_ids":["sec03-F18","sec03-F19","sec03-F20"]}],"narration":{"text":"The back seat is generally the safest place for children. If an older child must ride in the front, the vehicle seat should be moved as far back as it goes. To keep a child's head away from an inflating airbag, use a restraint with a full harness, or a properly fitted shoulder and lap belt. Passengers who are unbuckled, or who sit too close to an airbag, can be badly hurt even in a minor collision or a sudden stop. So distance and a proper belt work together: the further back and the better buckled, the safer the child.","fact_ids":["sec03-F18","sec03-F19","sec03-F20"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec03-u03-s5","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Infants and front airbags","fact_ids":["sec03-R06","sec03-F21","sec03-F18"]},"lines":[{"text":"Older child up front: only when needed.","fact_ids":["sec03-R06","sec03-F21","sec03-F18"]},{"text":"Infant in front of an airbag: never.","fact_ids":["sec03-R06","sec03-F21","sec03-F18"]},{"text":"Airbags burst out extremely fast.","fact_ids":["sec03-R06","sec03-F21","sec03-F18"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is the trap. Because an older child may ride in front when necessary with the seat pushed fully back, some people assume an infant can too, especially in a rear-facing seat. That is wrong. Never place an infant in the front seat of a car with a passenger-side airbag. The airbag bursts out of the dashboard at about two hundred miles per hour and can strike the back of the baby's head through the safety seat.
